blocks.md: This lesson follows **Model Cascades and Routing** in *Agent Economics* (Vol III).

blocks.source: Vol III, Agent Economics, § Model Cascades and Routing
blocks.md: Critical-path analysis shows where faster execution shortens a task, while routing decides which model configuration should attempt the work in the first place. Sending every ticket to a frontier model overpays on routine code transformations that a small, specialized model can complete at negligible cost, whereas sending every ticket to the small model fails on complex, ambiguous system bugs and multiplies retry and triage costs.

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why Cohort cost per accepted task matters for the system this section describes.
blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: Measured cost per accepted task is the sum of every initiated task's account, each charge in exactly one category, divided by the distinct tasks accepted under one declared contract.

questions.q: The section **Model Cascades and Routing** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Measured cost per accepted task is the sum of every initiated task's account, each charge in exactly one category, divided by the distinct tasks accepted under one declared contract.

Accepted tasks per unit time is the platform's deliverable, so sustaining goodput G at acceptance alpha requires admitting G/alpha trajectories and any change that lowers acceptance raises offered load.

Deterministic code, a fixed workflow, a bounded loop, and delegation are compared under one acceptance contract by cost per resolved task including human fallback, not by automated cost per automated acceptance.

Ideal prefix reuse bills the quadratic re-send at the cached rate, which lowers its coefficient without removing it, so a compaction pays back only after enough turns to recover its rewrite and lost cache.
